tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.
The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.
It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.
It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.
The trail was too steep for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike.**

After an adjective, enough sits in the final slot before a purpose infinitive. Hot enough to warm us puts the quality first and the sufficiency marker second, which is the everyday pattern for "sufficiently hot." The rest of the sentence simply names what that heat achieved after the hike.

Adjective before enough before to… is the sufficiency order here, so the wording is true.

**B) The soup was enough hot to warm us after the hike.**

Enough cannot come before an adjective when you mean "sufficiently hot." As written, enough hot reverses the required order and sounds ungrammatical in careful English. Flip the pair to hot enough, or change the meaning entirely to too hot if you intend excess rather than sufficiency.

Enough before an adjective reverses the required pair, so this is false — "The soup was hot enough to warm us after the hike."

**C) It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk.**

Such intensifies a whole noun phrase, not a lone adjective. Such a noisy café that… correctly packages article, adjective, and singular countable noun before the result clause. The that-clause then reports what followed from that intensity.

**Tip:** Such owns the noun phrase; so owns the adjective (or adverb) alone.

Such owns the full countable noun phrase before that, so the sentence is true.

**D) It was so a noisy café that we could barely talk.**

So does not combine with an article before a noun. So a noisy café tries to treat so like such, and that blend is almost always wrong on exams. Either keep the noun under such (such a noisy café that…) or drop the noun and intensify only the adjective (so noisy that…).

So cannot take an article-plus-noun package the way such can, so the line is false; the true version is "It was such a noisy café that we could barely talk."

**E) The trail was too steep for beginners.**

Too + adjective marks excess relative to a purpose, audience, or limit. Too steep for beginners says the gradient goes past what beginners can handle, with for naming that audience. No extra much or noun-order tricks are needed for this clean frame.

Too + adjective + for… marks excess for that audience, so this line is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
These five lines swap so, such, too, and enough around everyday food, cafés, and hiking talk. You are deciding whether each sentence is grammatical as written—not whether you like the word choice.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The focus is partnering each intensifier with the right kind of word, and keeping enough after adjectives. So wants an adjective or adverb; such wants a noun phrase; too marks excess before an adjective; enough after an adjective signals "sufficient for a purpose." Easy misspellings of the pattern are really word-order errors: so a… and enough + adjective.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each letter, spot the intensifier first, then check what sits immediately after it. If the partner type or order is wrong, mark false; if the classic pattern holds (adj + enough, such a + noun, too + adj), mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.
There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.
He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.
He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The fog was so thick that the ferry stayed in harbour.**

So intensifies an adjective and can link a that-clause naming the result. So thick that… keeps only the adjective in so’s slot — the ferry outcome follows as consequence, not as a noun after so. The structure reads as ordinary cause-and-result English.

So + adjective + that cleanly pairs degree with consequence, so the wording is true.

**B) There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early.**

Such partners with a noun phrase; excitement is uncountable, so no a/an appears. There was such excitement that… intensifies the mass noun and lets that introduce what the intensity caused. The existential there was frame is a natural host for this pattern.

Such + uncountable noun needs no article, so the excitement line is true.

**C) There was so excitement that the crowd started cheering early.**

So cannot modify a bare noun the way such can. So excitement leaves so without its usual adjective, adverb, or much/many partner. Repair by switching intensifier (such excitement) or by quantifying (so much excitement that…).

Bare so before a noun leaves so without its partner, so this is false — "There was such excitement that the crowd started cheering early."

**D) He is not tall enough for the roller coaster.**

Under negation, enough still follows the adjective before for. Not tall enough for the roller coaster is the standard sufficiency check: height is measured against a requirement. The order adj + enough stays fixed even when not is present.

Not still leaves enough after the adjective before for, so the height check is true.

**E) He is not enough tall for the roller coaster.**

Enough tall flips the adjective–enough order that English requires here. Enough can precede a noun (enough time), but not an adjective of quality. Move enough after tall to restore the pattern under not.

Enough before tall flips the adjective–enough order, so the line is false; repair to "He is not tall enough for the roller coaster."
tasks.solution_overview:
Fog, ferry delays, crowd noise, and a roller-coaster height check — each sentence turns on so, such, or enough. Judge only the grammar of the intensifier pattern, not how dramatic the scene sounds.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Pair each intensifier with its partner: so with adjectives (and result that-clauses), such with nouns, and enough after adjectives before for / to…. When so sits bare before a noun with no much/many, the structure collapses.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan left to right for so / such / enough, then ask what word class follows. Correct partners stay true; so + bare noun or enough + adjective flips to false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.
It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.
The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.
The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.
She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty.**

Such an agrees with the vowel sound that begins early, then the singular noun train completes the phrase. Such an early train that… intensifies the whole noun phrase and adds a result clause about empty carriages. Article choice tracks sound, not a switch to so.

Such an + adjective + singular countable + that matches sound and count, so the wording is true.

**B) It was so an early train that half the carriages were empty.**

So an early train misassigns the article–noun package to so. Article plus noun belongs with such; so wants the adjective alone (so early that…) unless you use a special so adj a noun frame. As written, so an… is simply ungrammatical.

So an… misassigns the article–noun package, so this is false — "It was such an early train that half the carriages were empty."

**C) The suitcase is too heavy to lift alone.**

Too + adjective + to-infinitive expresses excess that blocks a result. Too heavy to lift alone means the weight stops a solo lift — "too heavy to…" → "so… that not…." The infinitive names the blocked action without needing for + object here.

**Tip:** "Too…to…" → "so…that not."

Too + adjective + to… correctly blocks a solo lift, so the suitcase line is true.

**D) The lecture was too much technical for first-year students.**

Much does not sit between too and a lone adjective. Too technical is the right excess frame; too much belongs with nouns (too much noise, too much detail). Inserting much before technical is a common mix of those two patterns.

**Trap:** too much technical looks intensified but crosses the adjective/noun line.

Much cannot sit between too and a lone adjective, so the lecture is false; the true version is "The lecture was too technical for first-year students."

**E) She sang so beautifully that the hall went silent.**

So can intensify adverbs of manner just as it intensifies adjectives. So beautifully that… grades how she sang and links the hush that followed. No noun is wrongly parked in so’s slot.

So + adverb + that intensifies manner the same way so + adjective does, so this line is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Early trains, heavy suitcases, technical lectures, and a quiet hall after a song — the sentences lean on such, so, and too. Your job is to accept clean patterns and reject article or much mistakes.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch article choice with such (such an before a vowel sound) and the too much trap before a lone adjective. So an… is never a substitute for such an…, and so + adverb + that is fine when you intensify manner.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see so / such before an article + noun, ask whether such owns that noun phrase. If too is followed by much + adjective (not a noun), mark false; keep too + adj + to and so + adverb + that as true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.
The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.
She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.
The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.
The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We had enough daylight to finish photographing the mural.**

When enough quantifies, it comes before the noun it measures. Enough daylight treats daylight as the resource of which there was a sufficient amount, then to… states the purpose. That noun slot is different from the adjective + enough frame used for qualities.

**Tip:** Enough + noun quantifies; adjective + enough grades a quality.

Enough before a noun quantifies the resource before to…, so the daylight wording is true.

**B) The path was so icy that cyclists walked their bikes.**

So + adjective + that builds degree and consequence in one stroke. Icy fills the adjective slot after so, and the that-clause reports what riders did as a result. Nothing from a noun-phrase pattern is forced into so’s place.

So + adjective + that builds degree and result without a noun intrusion, so the icy path is true.

**C) She typed so quickly notes that nobody could read them.**

So quickly should lead into that (or a similar result linker), not into a bare noun. Parking notes right after the adverb mixes the manner pattern with a noun-phrase pattern. Either finish the adverb route (so quickly that…) or rebuild under such (such quick notes that…).

So + adverb must lead into that, not a bare noun, so this is false — "She typed so quickly that nobody could read them."

**D) The film was such gripping that we stayed until the credits.**

Such needs a noun head to intensify; gripping alone is only an adjective. Without a film (or similar noun) after the adjective, such has nothing to attach to before that. Restore the noun phrase: such a gripping film that…

Such needs a noun head after the adjective, so the film line is false; rewrite as "The film was such a gripping film that we stayed until the credits."

**E) The kitchen is large enough for a second fridge.**

Adjective + enough + for + noun phrase is a standard sufficiency shape. Large enough places enough after the quality, and for a second fridge names what the space must accommodate. The same enough could also license to + verb when purpose is verbal rather than for + noun.

Adjective + enough + for… measures space against what it must hold, so the kitchen line is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Daylight for photography, icy paths, typing speed, a gripping film, and kitchen space — again so / such / enough decide truth. Separate quantity enough from adjective enough before you judge hybrids.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Enough + noun quantifies (enough daylight); adjective + enough describes sufficiency of a quality. Hybrid errors stack words from different patterns: so + adverb + noun, or such + bare adjective with no noun head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether enough is quantifying a noun or finishing an adjective. Then check that so's next word is adj/adv only, and that such still has a noun phrase before that.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.
There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.
The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.
The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.
It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There was so much rain that the cricket match was abandoned.**

When so grades quantity of an uncountable noun, much is the required intermediary. So much rain that… pairs much with mass rain and lets that state the abandoned match. Bare so rain would be impossible; much supplies the missing link.

**Tip:** Uncountable → so much; plural countable → so many.

So much + uncountable + that supplies the missing quantity link, so the rain wording is true.

**B) There were so many volunteers that the charity ran out of badges.**

Plural countable nouns take many, not much, under so. So many volunteers that… matches the count noun and reports the badge shortage as result. Subject–verb agreement with there were also fits the plural volunteers.

So many + plural countable matches volunteer count, so the charity line is true.

**C) The recipe is too vaguely to follow without a video.**

After linking be, too should grade an adjective that describes the subject. Too vaguely uses an adverb where too vague is needed: the recipe itself is vague, not "vaguely." The to-infinitive then names what the excess prevents.

**Trap:** -ly after be looks polished but is the wrong word class for a subject complement.

After be, too needs an adjective complement, not an adverb, so this is false — "The recipe is too vague to follow without a video."

**D) The offer was not generous enough to tempt her back.**

Enough still follows the adjective under negation before a purpose infinitive. Not generous enough to tempt her back means the offer failed the sufficiency test for bringing her back. This not + adj + enough to… shape is a frequent exam pattern.

Not + adjective + enough + to… still follows the post-adjective order, so the offer line is true.

**E) It was such bad weather that the outdoor market closed early.**

Such + adjective + uncountable noun needs no article before the mass noun. Such bad weather that… intensifies the noun phrase weather and states the market’s early close. Adding a would wrongly treat weather as a singular countable here.

**Tip:** Such bad weather / such good news — no a/an with the mass noun.

Such + adjective + uncountable noun drops a/an correctly, so the weather wording is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Rain, volunteers, a vague recipe, a job offer, and bad weather — quantity so much/many and such with uncountables sit beside a too + adverb slip. Count the noun before you choose much or many.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When so modifies quantity, check much (uncountable) versus many (plural countable). When too follows be, prefer an adjective describing the subject. Such before an uncountable noun phrase usually drops the article.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify whether the intensifier is grading quantity, quality, or excess. So much / so many + matching noun stays true; too + -ly after be when you mean the thing itself is false; adj + enough and such + adj + uncountable noun stay true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.
The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.
We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.
It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.
The library was enough quiet for evening revision.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The app loads too slowly to be useful during live quizzes.**

Too can grade an adverb of manner before a to-infinitive of blocked purpose. Too slowly to be useful parallels too small to…, only the word being intensified is an adverb because loads is verbal. The live-quiz context simply spells out when usefulness fails.

Too + adverb + to… marks excess manner blocking usefulness, so the app wording is true.

**B) The photos were such blurry that we deleted the whole roll.**

Such blurry leaves such without a noun head after the adjective. Either add the noun (such blurry photos that…) or switch intensifier to so (so blurry that…). As written, such has nothing substantial to intensify before that.

**Trap:** Bare such + adjective is a near-miss for such + adj + noun.

Such before a bare adjective has no noun to intensify, so this is false — "The photos were so blurry that we deleted the whole roll."

**C) We do not have enough flour to bake a second loaf.**

Enough before an uncountable noun quantifies the ingredient, not a quality. Enough flour to bake… measures how much flour is available for a second loaf. Negation with do not have leaves that noun–enough order unchanged.

Enough before an uncountable noun measures quantity under negation, so the flour line is true.

**D) It was so narrow a bridge that only one car could cross.**

So + adjective + a + noun + that is a formal but grammatical twin of such a + adj + noun. The article lands after the adjective: so narrow a bridge, not so a narrow bridge. Meaning matches such a narrow bridge while keeping the so…a… order.

**Tip:** So adj a noun → such a adj noun; both appear in careful English.

Formal so + adjective + a + noun puts the article after the adjective, so the bridge line is true.

**E) The library was enough quiet for evening revision.**

Quiet is an adjective, so enough must follow it, not precede it. Enough quiet is the same order error as enough hot; the repair is quiet enough for evening revision. Save enough before a word only when that word is a noun being quantified.

Enough before quiet is the same illegal order as enough hot, so the library is false; repair to "The library was quiet enough for evening revision."
tasks.solution_overview:
Slow apps, blurry photos, baking flour, a narrow bridge, and a quiet library — patterns range from everyday too…to… to the formal so + adj + a + noun. Do not mark a rarer formal pattern false just because such a… is more common.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch for such + bare adjective (needs a noun) and enough + adjective (must flip). Too + adverb + to is fine when manner is excessive, and enough + uncountable noun is the quantity slot.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check each intensifier's partner word class. Accept so narrow a bridge as a formal twin of such a narrow bridge; fail enough quiet and such blurry that…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.
It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.
The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.
Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.
The essay is too much short for a full literature review.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The deadline is tight enough that any delay will cost us the slot.**

Adjective + enough can take a that-clause as well as a to-infinitive. Tight enough that… still means "sufficiently tight," with that spelling out the consequence for delays. The result reading does not require flipping enough before the adjective.

Adjective + enough + that… still means sufficiently tight with a stated result, so the deadline wording is true.

**B) It was so clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late.**

A singular countable noun after so + adjective normally needs the article in the formal so adj a noun shape — or you must switch to such a…. So clever puzzle drops that patterning and leaves puzzle looking stranded. Use such a clever puzzle that… or so clever that… without forcing the noun after so in this incomplete way.

**Trap:** So + adj + countable noun without a is a classic exam miss.

So + adjective + countable noun needs article patterning (or such a…), so this is false — "It was such a clever puzzle that the whole class stayed late."

**C) The courier arrived too late for us to catch the evening train.**

Too + adjective/adverb + for + object + to-infinitive packages excess relative to someone’s ability. Too late for us to catch… means we could not catch the evening train in time. The for…to… complement is fully licensed after too.

**Tip:** Too late for X to V → X cannot V in time.

Too…for…to… packages excess against someone’s ability, so the courier line is true.

**D) Such were the crowds that the museum opened an extra wing.**

Inversion after such (such were the crowds that…) is literary but grammatical. Such still intensifies the noun phrase the crowds; only the be-verb and subject swap places for emphasis. Unusual word order alone is not a reason to mark the line false.

**Tip:** Such + be + noun phrase + that is formal style, not an error.

Literary inversion still leaves such intensifying the crowds before that, so the museum line is true.

**E) The essay is too much short for a full literature review.**

Much again invades the too + adjective slot where it does not belong. Too short is the excess frame; too much short confuses that with too much + noun. Drop much and leave too directly before the adjective.

Much does not belong between too and a short adjective, so the essay is false; the true version is "The essay is too short for a full literature review."
tasks.solution_overview:
Deadlines, puzzles, late couriers, museum crowds, and short essays — most items still hinge on so/such/too word order, but one formal inversion with such is legitimately correct. Unusual word order is not automatically wrong.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep policing partners of so and the too much + adjective error. Adj + enough + that is acceptable, and such were the crowds that… is literary inversion, not a slip. So + adj + countable noun without a remains a classic miss.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept tight enough that… and the inverted such were…. Fail so clever puzzle (missing article patterning) and too much short (much before an adjective).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.
They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.
They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.
The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.
We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The map was not clear enough for hikers to follow in mist.**

Not + adjective + enough can license for + noun + to-infinitive. Not clear enough for hikers to follow… means it failed the sufficiency test for misty navigation. Enough sits after clear even though the complement is longer than a bare for-phrase.

Not + adjective + enough + for…to… keeps enough after the adjective, so the map wording is true.

**B) They made so rapid progress that the language course finished early.**

Progress is uncountable, so so + adjective + noun can appear without a. So rapid progress that… contrasts with countable failures like so clever puzzle, which need article patterning. The that-clause states the early finish as result.

**Tip:** So + adj + uncountable noun can work; countable singulars usually need a or such a….

So + adjective + uncountable noun can sit before that without an article, so rapid progress is true.

**C) They made such rapid progress that the language course finished early.**

Such + adjective + uncountable noun is the safer textbook twin of the previous line. Such rapid progress that… intensifies the noun phrase without an article before mass progress. Many exam keys prefer this default when both so… and such… are possible.

Such + adjective + uncountable noun is the textbook twin of that pattern, so the progress line is true.

**D) The backpack is too heavily to carry up the ridge.**

After linking be, the subject backpack needs an adjective complement, not an adverb of manner. Too heavily belongs with how someone carries; too heavy describes the bag itself before to carry…. Word-class slips after be are a frequent trap beside the familiar too…to shape.

**Trap:** Too + -ly after be looks parallel to too slowly loads… but wrong for a subject complement.

After be, too wants an adjective about the bag, not an adverb of manner, so this is false — "The backpack is too heavy to carry up the ridge."

**E) We kept enough spare batteries to last the whole festival.**

Enough here quantifies a noun phrase (spare batteries), not a bare adjective. Enough spare batteries means a sufficient number of that kind for the festival’s length. This is not the illegal enough + adjective flip; a noun head follows enough.

Enough before a noun phrase quantifies batteries, not a bare adjective, so the festival stock is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Misty hiking maps, language progress, overloaded backpacks, and spare batteries — countable versus uncountable after so/such matters, and be still wants an adjective after too. Enough before a noun phrase is not the enough + adjective error.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Distinguish countable vs uncountable after so/such, and adjective vs adverb after linking be. So + adj + uncountable noun (so rapid progress) can work; such rapid progress is the safer twin. Too heavily after be is the wrong word class.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the noun is uncountable, both so adj + noun and such adj + noun may be true. Fail adverbials after be where an adjective describes the subject; accept not + adj + enough for…to… and enough + noun phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.
The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.
It was too a complicated route for a first visit.
There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.**

So + adjective + as to + infinitive is a formal result pattern parallel to so…that. So stunning as to stop us means the view was stunning enough that it stopped us mid-sentence. The infinitive carries the result; as to is the linker, not a freestanding as + clause.

**Tip:** So…as to… → so…that someone/something does…

So + adjective + as to + infinitive is a valid formal result twin of so…that, so the view wording is true.

**B) The view was such stunning as to stop us mid-sentence.**

Such does not take as to after a bare adjective. Such wants a noun phrase (such a stunning view that…), while so…as to pairs with adjectives. Mixing such stunning with as to stacks pieces from incompatible patterns.

**Trap:** Such…as to after a bare adjective is a polished-looking near-miss for so…as to.

Such cannot take a bare adjective before as to, so this is false — "The view was so stunning as to stop us mid-sentence."

**C) The oven is not hot enough to crisp the pastry.**

Not + adjective + enough + to… places enough after hot before the purpose infinitive. The oven fails the heat threshold needed to crisp the pastry. Participial or ordinary adjectives both keep enough in that post-adjective slot.

Not still parks enough after hot before the purpose infinitive, so the oven line is true.

**D) It was too a complicated route for a first visit.**

Too never takes the article immediately after it. Too a complicated… is ungrammatical; the formal repair places the adjective first (too complicated a route) or switches to such a complicated route. Article placement after too is the tell.

**Trap:** Too a… looks like a blend of too… and such a… and is never allowed.

Too never takes the article right after it, so the route is false; repair to "It was too complicated a route for a first visit."

**E) There has been such an upsurge in tickets that the box office stayed open late.**

Such an + singular countable noun intensifies a countable surge. Upsurge takes an, and the that-clause reports the late box-office hours. Present perfect there has been is a natural host for this noun-phrase pattern.

Such an + singular countable + that matches countable upsurge, so the ticket wording is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stunning views, pastry, complicated routes, and ticket surges — formal so…as to… enters alongside ordinary enough and such. Treat the elevated pattern as fair game when the pieces fit.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective + as to + infinitive parallels so…that for result. Such does not take as to after a bare adjective, and too never precedes the article directly (too a…). Such an + countable singular remains standard.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept so stunning as to… and hot enough / such an upsurge. Fail such stunning as to… and too a complicated…; remember the repair too complicated a route is possible, but too a… never is.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.
Fans left because the queue was such long.
We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.
The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.
She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The novel is too dense a book for a single weekend.**

Too + adjective + a + noun + for… is the formal excess twin of so adj a noun. Too dense a book places the article after the adjective and measures the book against a weekend timeframe. Meaning is roughly "an excessively dense book for that span."

**Tip:** Too dense a book → such a dense book, but with an excess reading.

Too + adjective + a + noun + for… formally marks excess relative to a weekend, so the novel wording is true.

**B) Fans left because the queue was such long.**

Such long is incomplete: such needs a noun head (such a long queue) or you must switch to so long that…. A bare adjective after such leaves the intensifier without a phrase to intensify. The causal because-clause does not repair that missing noun.

**Trap:** Bare such + adjective is a short, plausible-looking incomplete.

Such needs a noun head (or a switch to so…), so this is false — "Fans left because the queue was so long."

**C) We arrived early enough to claim seats near the stage.**

Enough follows adverbs of time and manner just as it follows adjectives. Early enough to claim seats means arrival was sufficiently early for that purpose. The to-infinitive names what sufficiency made possible.

Adverb + enough + to… mirrors adjective + enough for sufficiency of timing, so early arrival is true.

**D) The coach found the warm-up so rushed that she ordered another lap.**

In a find + object + complement frame, so still intensifies the adjective. So rushed that… grades the warm-up and links the coach’s response. Reporting structure around the pattern does not change so’s partner word class.

So + adjective + that still works inside a find-complement, so the warm-up line is true.

**E) She is enough experienced to lead the climbing group.**

Experienced is an adjective, so enough must follow it. Enough experienced repeats the enough hot order error; experienced enough to lead… is the repair. The purpose infinitive stays after the corrected adj + enough pair.

Enough before experienced flips the required order, so the climbing line is false; the true version is "She is experienced enough to lead the climbing group."
tasks.solution_overview:
Dense novels, long queues, early arrivals, rushed warm-ups, and climbing experience — formal too/so + adj + a + noun shapes appear beside the usual enough and such traps. Article placement after the adjective is the tell.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Accept too/so + adjective + a + noun when the article lands after the adjective. Reject such + bare adjective and enough + adjective, which recycle the same order mistakes from easier tasks.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you see too/so + adj + a + noun + for/that, treat it as formal but true. Fail such long without a noun, and flip enough experienced to experienced enough.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.
The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.
We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.
It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.
The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The storm was so fierce as that ferries cancelled sailings.**

Result after so allows that or as to, but not both markers stacked. So fierce as that mixes the as to infinitive route with a that-clause and collapses. Choose one linker: so fierce that… or so fierce as to force cancellations….

**Trap:** As that after so looks doubly "result-like" but is never a standard combination.

Result after so allows that or as to, not both stacked, so this is false — "The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings."

**B) The storm was so fierce that ferries cancelled sailings.**

This is the clean so + adjective + that result pattern with a single linker. Fierce sits alone after so, and that introduces the cancelled sailings. No as is competing for the same result slot.

A single that after so + adjective keeps cause and result clean, so the fierce-storm wording is true.

**C) We lacked enough evidence to challenge the referee's call.**

Enough before an uncountable noun quantifies how much evidence was available. Enough evidence to challenge… states that the amount fell short of what a challenge required. Uncountables take the same enough + noun slot as flour or time.

Enough before an uncountable noun measures how much evidence there was, so the referee line is true.

**D) It was such a poorly printed map that hikers took wrong turns.**

Such can head a heavily modified noun phrase: adverb + adjective + noun still sits under such a. Poorly modifies printed inside the noun phrase; the whole noun phrase is what such intensifies. The that-clause reports the navigational result.

**Tip:** Such a poorly printed X still counts as a noun phrase after such.

Such can head a noun phrase even when adverb + adjective modify the noun, so the map line is true.

**E) The hills are too steep for the juniors finish before dusk.**

After for + object, the next verb needs to before the infinitive. Too steep for the juniors finish… drops that to; the repair is for the juniors to finish before dusk. The too + adjective frame is otherwise intact.

**Trap:** Missing to after for + object is easy to overlook beside an otherwise clean too… pattern.

For + object needs to before the infinitive, so the juniors line is false; repair to "The hills are too steep for the juniors to finish before dusk."
tasks.solution_overview:
Fierce storms, referee disputes, poorly printed maps, and steep hills for juniors — blended result markers and a missing to after for + object are the hard catches. Such can still head a heavily modified noun phrase.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hunt stacked linkers after so (as that mixes two patterns) and missing to in too…for X [to] V. Enough + noun before to remains the quantity pattern; such a + adverb + adjective + noun is fine when everything modifies the noun head.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Choose exactly one result linker after so: that or as to, never as that. Keep enough evidence and such a poorly printed map; add to before finish in the juniors line.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.
Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.
The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.
There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.
The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Practice stopped because the heat became so intense.**

So + adjective can stand without an explicit that-clause when context already implies the result. Because practice stopped supplies that consequence, so intense does not need another that. Optional result clauses after so/such/too/enough are common but not obligatory.

Bare so + adjective is true when because already supplies the result, so the heat wording is true.

**B) Practice stopped because the heat became such intense.**

Such intense needs a noun (such intense heat) or a switch to so intense. After become, a subject complement is typically so + adjective, not bare such + adjective. The because-clause does not supply the missing noun head.

**Trap:** Such intense looks parallel to so intense but leaves such without a noun.

Such before a standalone adjective still needs a noun, so this is false — "Practice stopped because the heat became so intense."

**C) The clause is worded carefully enough to avoid confusion.**

Enough follows the adverb carefully that grades how the clause is worded. Carefully enough to avoid confusion works like adjective + enough + to… for manner. The purpose infinitive names what that careful wording achieves.

Adverb + enough + to… grades manner against a purpose, so the clause wording is true.

**D) There were too few lifeguards to watch every lane.**

Too few + plural noun expresses an excess of scarcity — roughly "not enough." Too few lifeguards to watch every lane is grammatical; too few is not the illegal too much + adjective error. The infinitive states what the shortage prevents.

**Tip:** Too few → not enough in meaning; the grammar still uses too + few + plural noun.

Too few + plural noun + to… is a grammatical scarcity frame, so the lifeguard line is true.

**E) The gallery hung so few paintings that the room felt empty.**

So few + plural countable + that parallels so many in structure. Few grades small quantity the way many grades large quantity under so. The that-clause reports the sparse, empty feel of the room.

So few + plural countable + that parallels so many for small quantity, so the gallery wording is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Intense heat stopping practice, careful wording, short staffing of lifeguards, and a sparse gallery wall — result that-clauses are optional here. The real test is whether such has a noun and whether few sits correctly after so/too.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective can stand alone when context implies the result. Such still needs a noun head after become. Too few / so few + plural noun are grammatical quantity patterns, not the too much + adjective error.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If such + adjective has no noun, mark false. Accept bare so intense, carefully enough to…, too few lifeguards, and so few paintings that…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.
The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.
Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.
She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.
The trail is not enough marked for night walking.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour.**

Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern with no adjective after such. The rule is such that… means the nature of the rule produces that waiting outcome. Here such that is not interchangeable with purpose so that.

**Tip:** Noun + is such that… → the nature of X means / brings about…

Formal noun + is such that… means of a kind that, so the tour-rule wording is true.

**B) The rule is so that latecomers wait for the next tour.**

So that primarily marks purpose ("in order that"), not "of a kind that." Saying the rule is so that… tries to borrow such that’s character reading and misfires. If the point is what the rule’s nature entails, such that is required.

**Trap:** So that and such that look related but do different jobs after a noun + be.

Purpose so that cannot do the “of a kind that” job after is, so this is false — "The rule is such that latecomers wait for the next tour."

**C) Runners pulled out, the course having become too muddy to race.**

Too + adjective + to-infinitive keeps its shape inside a participial absolute. The course having become too muddy to race explains why runners pulled out, with too…to still marking blocked racing. Reduced clause packaging does not cancel the excess pattern.

Too…to… keeps its excess shape inside a participial absolute, so the muddy-course line is true.

**D) She left enough of a gap to let the next cyclist pass.**

Enough of a + singular countable noun is an idiomatic quantifying frame. Enough of a gap to… means a sufficient gap for the next rider to pass. The of a(n) piece is natural before singular count nouns in this pattern.

**Tip:** Enough of a gap / enough of an issue — of a(n) before singular count nouns.

Enough of a + singular countable is the idiomatic quantifying frame, so the cycling gap is true.

**E) The trail is not enough marked for night walking.**

Marked is adjectival here, so enough must follow it even under negation. Not enough marked reverses the order; not marked enough for night walking is the repair. Not does not license parking enough before the adjective.

**Trap:** Negation makes the enough + adjective error feel slightly less obvious.

Negation still leaves enough after the adjective, so the trail is false; rewrite as "The trail is not marked enough for night walking."
tasks.solution_overview:
Tour rules, muddy race courses, bike gaps, and marked trails — harder items separate such that (nature/result) from so that (purpose), and test enough of a… plus adjective–enough order under negation.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Such that meaning "of a kind that" is a fixed formal pattern. So that marks purpose ("in order that") and cannot swap in for that reading. Enough of a + singular countable noun is idiomatic; enough still follows adjectives even with not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the clause describes the nature of the rule (such that) or a purpose (so that). Accept too…to inside reduced clauses and enough of a gap; flip not enough marked to not marked enough.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.
Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts.
The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student.
We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists.
The rebuild was enough extensive that the gallery closed for a year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Attendance fell so low as volunteers began cancelling shifts.**

A finite result clause after so + adjective wants that, not bare as. So low as volunteers… is not the standard result pattern; so low as to cause cancellations would need the infinitive after as to. As written, as + finite clause after so + adj is the wrong linker set.

**Trap:** So…as + finite clause mimics so…as to… but drops the required to + infinitive.

A finite result after so + adjective wants that (or as to + infinitive), so this is false — "Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts."

**B) Attendance fell so low that volunteers began cancelling shifts.**

So + adjective + that is the default result pattern for this meaning. Low is graded by so, and that introduces the volunteer cancellations. One clear linker keeps the cause–result reading unambiguous.

So + adjective + that is the default result linker set, so the attendance wording is true.

**C) The visa proved too costly a requirement for the exchange student.**

Too + adjective + a + noun + for… is formal excess English. Too costly a requirement places the article after the adjective and measures cost against the student. Meaning is an excessively costly requirement for that person.

Too + adjective + a + noun + for… formally marks excess cost, so the visa line is true.

**D) We cannot cook without such spices as the recipe lists.**

Such…as can mean "the kind that," with a relative-like follow-on. "Such spices as the recipe lists" → "the spices that the recipe lists." This formal matching pattern is distinct from result such…that.

**Tip:** "Such N as X lists" → "the N that X lists."

Such…as in the “kind that” reading equates the listed spices, so that frame is true.

**E) The rebuild was enough extensive that the gallery closed for a year.**

Enough extensive reverses adjective–enough order before a that-clause. The repair is extensive enough that…; enough never precedes the adjective in this sufficiency frame. The gallery result does not excuse the word-order error.

Enough before extensive reverses adjective–enough order, so the rebuild is false; the true version is "The rebuild was extensive enough that the gallery closed for a year."
tasks.solution_overview:
Falling attendance, costly visas, listed spices, and a long rebuild — result linkers after so, formal too adj a noun, and such…as all appear. Enough + adjective is still illegal.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate result that from faulty so…as + finite clause. Formal such…as ("the kind that") and too + adjective + a + noun are acceptable. Keep policing enough before adjectives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Default result linker after so is that (or as to + infinitive). Accept too costly a requirement and such spices as…; fail so low as volunteers… and enough extensive…

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.

tactical_explanations:
**A) The playlist was so arranged as to build toward the finale.**

So + past participle/adjective + as to + infinitive expresses designed or resulting manner. So arranged as to build… means arranged in such a way that it built toward the finale. Formal as to + infinitive carries the intended trajectory cleanly.

**Tip:** So arranged as to… → arranged in such a way that…

So + participle + as to + infinitive states designed manner or result, so the playlist wording is true.

**B) Cash on hand is barely enough for bus fare, let alone a taxi.**

Enough for + noun expresses sufficiency; barely only intensifies how tight that sufficiency is. Barely enough for bus fare keeps enough in its quantity role and contrasts with the larger taxi cost. Degree modifiers like barely or almost can precede enough without breaking the frame.

Barely can intensify enough for… without breaking sufficiency, so the fare line is true.

**C) It was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.**

Dummy it with too little + noun is awkward and typically marked wrong for this quantity reading. English prefers an existential or possessional frame: there was / we had too little time…. The remaining to rehearse… purpose is fine once the host clause is repaired.

**Trap:** It was too little time looks close to there was too little time but misuses dummy it.

Dummy it was too little time mishosts the shortage frame, so this is false — "There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act."

**D) There was too little time remaining to rehearse the second act.**

There was + too little + uncountable noun is the natural existential shortage pattern. Too little time remaining to rehearse… frames the deficit cleanly before the blocked purpose. This is the repair target the previous letter fails to reach.

There was + too little + noun + to… is the natural existential shortage pattern, so rehearsal time is true.

**E) The dish became such favourite with locals that tourists queued daily.**

Favourite is a singular countable here, so such needs an article: such a favourite. Omitting a leaves such favourite incomplete before the that-clause about tourist queues. Alternatively, rebuild without such’s noun demand (so popular with locals that…).

**Trap:** Missing a/an after such with a countable singular is a high-frequency slip.

Singular countable favourite after such needs a/an, so the dish is false; repair to "The dish became such a favourite with locals that tourists queued daily."
tasks.solution_overview:
Playlists, bus fare, rehearsal time, and a local favourite dish — existential framing with too little + noun and articles after such decide several letters. Surface similarity can hide a missing there or a/an.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Judge there was / we had with too little + noun, article requirements after such with countable singulars, and formal so…as to…. Barely can intensify enough without breaking the pattern.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer there-insertion with too little/much + noun; fail dummy it was too little time…. Accept so arranged as to… and barely enough for…; add a before favourite.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.
The experiment is designed so that temperature stays constant.
The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing.
He spoke with so a confident tone that doubts faded.
We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The experiment is designed such that temperature stays constant.**

After verbs of designing or configuring, such that means "in such a way that." Designed such that temperature stays constant is standard scientific register. The clause after such that states the maintained condition, not a purpose clause in disguise.

**Tip:** Verb + such that → configured so that / in such a way that.

Designed such that… means configured so the condition holds, so the lab wording is true.

**B) The experiment is designed so that temperature stays constant.**

Designed so that… expressing purpose or intended result is also grammatical. Here so that and such that can both work, with so that leaning slightly more toward intended purpose. Neither linker is automatically wrong after designed.

Designed so that… as purpose or intended result is equally grammatical here, so that twin is true.

**C) The dough proved elastic enough that it stretched without tearing.**

Adjective + enough + that-clause remains acceptable for sufficiency with a stated consequence. Elastic enough that it stretched… means sufficiently elastic that stretching succeeded without tearing. Proved simply hosts the same adj + enough core.

Adjective + enough + that… marks sufficiency plus a stated stretch result, so the dough line is true.

**D) He spoke with so a confident tone that doubts faded.**

So a confident tone wrongly places the article immediately after so. Inside a longer prepositional phrase the same ban holds: use such a confident tone or so confidently that…. So a… remains a trap even when the noun phrase is not the whole sentence.

**Trap:** So a… returns inside PPs and still fails the article test.

So cannot take the article immediately after it inside a PP either, so this is false — "He spoke with such a confident tone that doubts faded."

**E) We kept the talk short enough not to overrun the lunch break.**

Adjective + enough + not to-infinitive encodes avoidance via sufficiency. Short enough not to overrun means sufficiently short to avoid overrunning the lunch break. The negation attaches to the infinitive purpose, not to the enough order.

**Tip:** Enough not to… → sufficiently… to avoid…

Adjective + enough + not to… encodes avoidance through sufficiency, so the talk length is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Lab temperature control, elastic dough, confident speaking, and a short talk — after verbs of designing, both so that and such that can be right. The old so a… trap still fails.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Designed such that… ("in such a way that") and designed so that… (purpose/result) are both grammatical with slightly different nuance. Adj + enough + that and enough not to… are valid; so a… is not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow both designing linkers when the sentence is well formed. Fail so a confident tone; accept elastic enough that… and short enough not to…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.
The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.
Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.
The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.
They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Seldom is a coastline so eroded that no beach remains.**

Fronted seldom triggers inversion, but the inner so + adjective + that pattern stays intact. So eroded that no beach remains is still the core you judge; the inversion shell does not break it. Advanced packaging around a clean intensifier pattern remains true.

**Tip:** Judge the so/such/too/enough core even inside inversion shells.

Seldom-inversion leaves the inner so + adjective + that core intact, so the coastline wording is true.

**B) The tent proved insufficiently sturdy enough to survive the gale.**

Insufficiently and enough both mark sufficiency, so stacking them doubles the tool. Use insufficiently sturdy or not sturdy enough — not both on one adjective phrase. The gale purpose infinitive cannot rescue the double marking.

**Trap:** Insufficiently…enough looks thorough but overloads the same semantic job.

Insufficiently and enough double-mark sufficiency on one phrase, so this is false — "The tent proved not sturdy enough to survive the gale."

**C) Her complaint was not so much unfair as poorly timed.**

Not so much X as Y is an established correlative idiom that requires so. The line compares two evaluations rather than intensifying unfair in the ordinary so + adjective sense. Idiom status makes the so grammatical even though this is not classic degree so…that.

**Tip:** Not so much…as… is a correlative idiom, not ordinary so + adjective intensification.

Not so much…as… is a correlative idiom that legitimately uses so, so the complaint line is true.

**D) The delay was such that, had we waited, the concert would have started.**

Such that can introduce complex follow-ons, including an inverted counterfactual. The delay was such that… still means "of a kind / degree that," and the had we waited clause continues formally. Complexity after such that is not itself an error.

Such that can host a complex inverted conditional follow-on, so the delay wording is true.

**E) They priced the tickets too steeply for students to attend weekly.**

Too + adverb + for + noun + to-infinitive marks excess manner or pricing. Too steeply for students to attend… parallels too steep for X to V, with the adverb modifying priced. Whether you need adverb or adjective depends on what is being modified; here the verb pricing takes the adverb.

Too + adverb + for…to… marks excess pricing manner, so the student-ticket line is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Eroded coastlines, gale-hit tents, timed complaints, delayed concerts, and steep ticket prices — advanced packaging wraps familiar so/such/too cores in inversion and idioms. Reject double intensifiers; keep legitimate so idioms.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Inversion shells and correlative not so much…as… still hide a clean so/such/too/enough core you can judge. Insufficiently…enough doubles sufficiency marking. Too + adverb + for…to… remains available for excess manner or cost.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Judge the inner pattern even when seldom opens the sentence. Fail stacked insufficiently sturdy enough; accept not so much…as…, such that with a counterfactual continuation, and too steeply for students to…

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other runner moved so swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.
No other runner moved such swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.

**A) No other runner moved so swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.**

So + adverb + as to + infinitive states result after a comparative or exclusive frame. So swiftly as to claim the lead works with adverbs the same way so stunning as to… works with adjectives. The no other runner frame does not disturb the so…as to core.

So + adverb + as to + infinitive parallels the adjective as-to frame, so the overnight-lead wording is true.

**B) No other runner moved such swiftly as to claim the lead overnight.**

Such does not modify adverbs; such swiftly is impossible. Such wants noun phrases (or the fixed such that), while so…as to pairs with adjectives and adverbs. Switch to so swiftly as to… or rebuild with a noun under such.

**Trap:** Such + adverb is a near-miss for so + adverb + as to.

Such cannot modify an adverb, so this is false — "No other runner moved so swiftly as to claim the lead overnight."

**C) The rule is drawn tightly enough that substitutions need consent.**

Adverb + enough + that remains grammatical in careful register. Tightly enough that… means sufficiently tightly that substitutions need consent. Enough stays after the adverb before the result clause.

Adverb + enough + that remains grammatical for sufficiency plus result, so the consent rule is true.

**D) We had rather too little daylight for a full summit attempt.**

Rather too is an idiomatic softener before an excess/scarcity phrase. Rather too little daylight for a full summit attempt means somewhat excessively little light for that attempt. Degree modifiers like rather, a bit, or far can sit before too.

**Tip:** Rather / a bit / far can modify too.

Rather too little + noun softens excess scarcity idiomatically, so the summit daylight is true.

**E) The interface was so intuitive a design as users needed no tutorial.**

So adj a noun pairs with that or as to, not with bare as + finite clause. So intuitive a design as users… mismatches; use that…, or as to need…. The formal article-after-adjective shape is fine — only the linker is wrong.

**Trap:** So adj a noun as + finite clause blends two result patterns incorrectly.

So adj a noun needs that or as to, not bare as + finite clause, so the interface is false; rewrite as "The interface was so intuitive a design that users needed no tutorial."
highlights: so intuitive a design as users
tasks.solution_overview:
Overnight race leads, tightly drawn rules, thin daylight, and intuitive interfaces — stress-test so…as to… with adverbs and demand the right linker after so adj a noun. Degree modifiers before too are allowed.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adverb + as to + infinitive works; such does not modify adverbs. Adv/adj + enough + that remains fine in careful register. Rather too… is idiomatic; so adj a noun needs that or as to, not bare as + finite clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept so swiftly as to…, tightly enough that…, and rather too little…. Fail such swiftly and so intuitive a design as users… (use that or as to need…).

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

**A) Only then did the river become high enough for kayaking to look safe.**

Only then did… inverts the subject and auxiliary, but high enough for… stays intact. Embedded enough patterns survive fronting and inversion when the adjective–enough order is kept. Kayaking to look safe is the for-complement measuring sufficiency.

Only-then inversion leaves high enough for… intact, so the kayaking wording is true.

**B) The study was based on so biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.**

So + adjective + a + noun + that works even inside a prepositional phrase. So biased a sample keeps the article after the adjective and links the collapsed conclusions. Meaning matches such a biased sample while preserving the formal so…a… order.

**Tip:** So biased a sample → such a biased sample in force.

So + adjective + a + noun + that stays valid inside a prepositional phrase, so the sample line is true.

**C) The study was based on such biased a sample that the conclusions collapsed.**

After such, the article must precede the adjective: such a biased sample. Such biased a sample borrows so/too article placement (adj + a + noun). Never write such + adj + a + noun; that order belongs to so/too, not such.

Adjective + enough and too + adjective can contrast cleanly in one sentence, so that coordination is true.

**Tip:** Too much of a X to V → excessively X-like to V.

Too much of a + noun + to… is the fixed evaluative idiom, so the perfectionist wording is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Kayaking on a high river, biased samples, thin supplies, and perfectionists — article placement separates so adj a noun (correct) from such adj a noun (incorrect). The idiom too much of a… to… is also in play.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

So + adjective + a + noun keeps the article after the adjective; such wants such a + adjective + noun. Embedded enough patterns survive inversion. Enough and too can contrast in one sentence; too much of a + noun + to… is a fixed evaluative idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept high enough inside only then did…, so biased a sample, healthy enough / too thin, and too much of a perfectionist to…. Fail such biased a sample (article must precede the adjective after such).

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had the ice been thick enough, the skaters would have crossed the lake.
The rehearsal grew so protracted as nobody could finalise the cues.
Whatever the poster promises, service is seldom swift enough to match it.
It remains too early a stage for full automation of bookings.
Their reply was so that we cancelled the booking at once.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Had the ice been thick enough, the skaters would have crossed the lake.**

Adjective + enough keeps its order inside an inverted third conditional. Had the ice been thick enough… still places enough after thick before the would have result. Conditional packaging does not move enough before the adjective.

Adjective + enough keeps its order inside an inverted conditional, so the ice wording is true.

**B) The rehearsal grew so protracted as nobody could finalise the cues.**

After so + adjective, a finite result clause needs that — or else as to + infinitive. So protracted as nobody… uses bare as + clause, which is not the standard result set. Repair with that… or as to prevent finalising…. 

**Trap:** So…as + finite clause is a recurring near-miss for so…that / so…as to.

So + adjective wants that or as to for result, not bare as + clause, so this is false — "The rehearsal grew so protracted that nobody could finalise the cues."

**C) Whatever the poster promises, service is seldom swift enough to match it.**

Seldom… enough to… correctly denies that the service reaches the poster’s promise. Swift enough keeps enough after the adjective; the frequency adverb does not disturb that order. The concessive whatever-clause is only scene-setting.

Seldom does not disturb adjective + enough + to… after the frequency adverb, so the poster line is true.

**D) It remains too early a stage for full automation of bookings.**

Too + adjective + a + noun + for… is formal but grammatical. Too early a stage places the article after early and measures the stage against full automation. Meaning is an excessively early stage for that goal.

Too + adjective + a + noun + for… formally places the article after early, so the booking stage is true.

**E) Their reply was so that we cancelled the booking at once.**

So that marks purpose ("in order that"), which does not fit a reply’s character or result. For nature/result after a noun + be, use such that we cancelled…, or intensify an adjective (so blunt that…). Purpose so that misreads what the reply caused or was like.

**Trap:** Reply/situation + so that is a near-miss for character/result such that.

Purpose so that cannot do character/result after was, so the reply is false; the true version is "Their reply was such that we cancelled the booking at once."
tasks.solution_overview:
Icy lakes, long rehearsals, poster promises, early booking automation, and abrupt replies — the final set mixes conditionals, formal too adj a noun, and result-linker discipline after so. Keep such that versus so that distinct.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Enough keeps adjective-final order even in had-conditionals. Results after so want that or as to, not as + finite clause. Too + adjective + a + noun (+ for…) is formal but correct; reply/situation + so that wrongly reads as purpose when character/result is meant.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept thick enough in the inverted conditional, swift enough to…, and too early a stage…. Fail so protracted as nobody… and was so that we… (use such that or so + adj + that).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
